Summary

This paper introduces a new task setting for product attribute mining in e-commerce: lightly supervised open-world attribute mining, where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover previously unseen attribute types without explicitly naming them at inference time. To support this setting, the authors construct a new dataset, WoaM, spanning four Amazon product categories and including titles and bullet-point descriptions. They propose Amacer, a pipeline with: (i) syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, (ii) supervised contrastive representation learning from a curated seed set, (iii) adaptive expansion of seed attributes plus DBSCAN clustering for remaining candidates, and (iv) two additional regularizers for unseen attribute discovery: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive loss and an unsupervised latent-attribute topic-model-like objective. Experiments show improvements over closed-world tagging baselines and OA-Mine-style open-world baselines.

Overall assessment

I think the paper tackles an important and practically relevant problem. The move from closed-world or zero-shot extraction toward automatic discovery of new attribute types is meaningful, and the paper is strongest when motivating why existing formulations are insufficient for realistic e-commerce settings. The dataset effort also appears substantial, especially the inclusion of bullet points rather than only titles. The empirical gains over baselines are promising, and the paper contains useful ablations and qualitative analysis.

That said, I also have several concerns. The main ones are around evaluation design, the novelty and necessity of some modeling components, and the degree to which the proposed setting is truly “open-world” versus “cluster unlabeled spans under weak supervision.” In particular, the main scalar metric (“pseudo-F1” derived from averaging Jaccard/ARI/NMI as pseudo precision) is unconventional and hard to interpret. Some methodological choices also seem heuristic and pipeline-dependent, making it difficult to know whether the gains come from the core learning formulation or from candidate generation and evaluation artifacts. I find the paper interesting and potentially publishable, but it would benefit from stronger justification and clearer analysis.

Strengths

1. Important problem setting
The paper addresses a realistic gap between closed-world extraction and zero-shot extraction with predefined target types. In practice, merchants and catalogs evolve quickly, and discovering new attributes without exhaustive annotation is valuable.

2. Practical dataset contribution
The WoaM dataset seems useful. Including both titles and bullet points is a meaningful improvement over title-only settings, and the paper convincingly argues that bullet points contain more unseen types and values.

3. Thoughtful weak supervision setup
The seed-set construction process is more careful than pure distant supervision. The hybrid sanitization plus light human curation is a reasonable compromise between scalability and quality.

4. Strong empirical improvements
Amacer improves substantially over the reported baselines, especially compared with OA-Mine variants. The decomposition into seed/new and title/bullet-point subsets is helpful.

5. Good qualitative discussion
The paper does not oversell the method and includes useful failure analysis, especially the tendency to absorb unseen types into semantically nearby seed types.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. Evaluation metric is unconventional and difficult to validate
The paper’s main metric is a “pseudo-F1” where the average of Jaccard, ARI, and NMI is treated as pseudo precision and combined with recall. This is not a standard clustering or extraction metric, and I am not convinced it is meaningful or calibrated. Jaccard, ARI, and NMI are not precision measures, and averaging them together before combining with recall seems arbitrary.

This matters because many of the paper’s headline gains are expressed in this metric. While the paper also reports the underlying clustering metrics and recall, the central claim of “+12 F1” depends on a derived score whose interpretation is unclear. I would strongly prefer either:
- standard clustering metrics reported separately without collapsing them into pseudo-F1, or
- a more principled end-task metric, e.g., span-level extraction precision/recall/F1 plus cluster/type discovery metrics.

2. The task definition still leaves ambiguity about what counts as a “new attribute type”
The annotation guideline says annotators label spans that are “reasonable attribute values” of either existing seed types or brand-new types that fit the context. This leaves substantial room for subjectivity. The paper acknowledges span-boundary subjectivity, but type granularity subjectivity may be even more serious. For example, when should “region of origin” be a new type versus part of ingredient/source/manufacturer/location? Since the task is open-world and cluster-based, annotation consistency on type granularity is crucial.

I would like to see inter-annotator agreement not only on spans but also on type induction/granularity. Without that, it is hard to know how stable the benchmark is.

3. Novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level
The overall framing is novel, but many components are combinations of known ideas:
- POS-pattern candidate generation,
- supervised contrastive learning over seed values,
- prototype/support-set thresholding,
- DBSCAN for residual clustering,
- skip-gram-like co-occurrence regularization,
- neural topic-model-inspired latent variables.

The contribution is therefore more in task formulation and system integration than in a sharply new algorithmic idea. That is acceptable, but then the paper should more clearly isolate which components are essential and why this particular combination is better than simpler alternatives.

4. Candidate generation may dominate performance
The syntax-based candidate generation appears to be a major source of gains over segmentation-based OA-Mine variants. This is not a problem in itself, but it complicates the claim that the representation learning and latent-attribute regularization are the main advances. The paper does include some comparisons controlling candidate generation, which is good, but I still think more analysis is needed.

For example:
- What is candidate recall against gold spans before clustering?
- How sensitive is performance to the POS tagger and pattern inventory?
- How much manual tuning of stopwords/pattern filtering was needed?
- How does a simpler noun-phrase chunker baseline compare?

5. The self-supervised heuristic is plausible but weakly justified
The assumption that spans within the same bullet point are semantically related and spans across bullet points of the same product are negatives is intuitive, but also noisy. In many product descriptions, a bullet point can mention multiple unrelated attributes, and different bullet points can discuss the same attribute. The paper acknowledges noise, but I would like more evidence that this heuristic helps for the intended reason rather than merely acting as generic regularization.

6. The latent attribute model is interesting but under-analyzed
The topic-model-inspired component is probably the most novel technical part, but it is also the least convincing empirically from the current presentation. The paper says it contributes around 70% of the regularization improvement, but there is limited detail in the main text. Important questions remain:
- How sensitive is performance to K, the number of latent attributes?
- How severe is topic collapse in practice?
- Does the latent model discover category-specific or cross-category concepts?
- Why is bag-of-spans reconstruction the right objective for attribute discovery rather than simply product-level contrastive learning?

7. Comparison to stronger modern baselines is limited
The baselines are reasonable relative to prior work, but the paper could compare against stronger generic alternatives. For example:
- sentence-transformer or SimCSE-style embeddings plus clustering,
- noun phrase extraction plus metric learning,
- prompt-based or instruction-tuned LLM extraction as a weak baseline,
- nearest-neighbor expansion from seed values without the latent module,
- constrained agglomerative clustering or HDBSCAN.

Given the practical framing, stronger non-specialized baselines would help establish that the gains are not mainly due to engineering choices.

8. Statistical significance claims are thin
The paper mentions t-test significance at >95% confidence for the best F1. With only four product categories and macro-averaging across them, it is unclear whether the sample size is sufficient for a meaningful t-test. More robust reporting, such as multiple random seeds and confidence intervals, would be preferable.

Detailed comments

1. Seed-set construction and leakage
The seed set is built from retailer-provided product profiles, then string-matched into the corpus for training. The test set uses additional products not covered in the raw corpus, which is good. Still, I would like a clearer statement about whether any seed values themselves appear in test products and whether this is considered acceptable. Since the task includes seed expansion, overlap in values is not necessarily leakage, but the exact split protocol should be explicit.

2. Adaptive thresholding
The threshold for assigning a candidate to a seed attribute is based on average pairwise cosine distance among seed values, scaled by delta. This is simple and intuitive, but potentially brittle when seed sets are small or heterogeneous. Some attributes naturally have broad semantics and low internal similarity. It would help to compare against learned thresholds or prototype variance models.

3. Representation of spans
The model averages token embeddings from BERT without additional encoding parameters. This simplicity is appealing, but perhaps too weak for long or compositional spans. Did the authors try span boundary markers, CLS pooling with span prompts, or SBERT-style pooling? Since the paper emphasizes representation learning, stronger span encoders would be relevant.

4. Closed-world baselines are somewhat disadvantaged
The paper compares open-world methods to tagging models that cannot discover new types by design. This supports the motivation, but the comparison is not entirely fair as an overall benchmark. The more informative comparisons are among open-world methods under matched candidate generation.

5. Exact vs partial span matching
I appreciate the inclusion of partial matching. However, the threshold “more than half of the span falls into a gold value” is asymmetric and may favor certain prediction lengths. Please clarify whether overlap is measured relative to predicted span, gold span, or both.

6. Dataset scale and diversity
The dataset covers four categories, which is a decent start, but still limited. It would help to know how much cross-category transfer is possible or whether models are trained separately per category. If trained per category, the open-world claim is mostly within-category discovery rather than broader generalization.

7. Naming and usability of discovered clusters
Since the output is clusters rather than named attributes, how would this be used in practice? Real catalog systems usually need canonical attribute names. The paper should discuss whether cluster naming is out of scope or whether seed-nearest labels / manual post-hoc naming would be required.

Questions for the authors

1. How consistent are annotators on new type induction and granularity, not just span selection?
2. Can you report standard extraction precision/recall/F1 by type category, in addition to clustering metrics and pseudo-F1?
3. How sensitive is Amacer to the number of latent attributes K and to the POS pattern inventory?
4. How much of the gain remains if candidate spans are generated by a generic noun-phrase chunker instead of your POS-pattern mining?
5. Are models trained separately for each category, or jointly across categories?
6. Can you provide ablations isolating self-supervised loss only vs latent-attribute loss only in the main paper?
7. How often do discovered “new” clusters correspond to coherent but annotation-mismatched refinements of seed types rather than truly novel types?

Suggestions for improvement

1. Rework the evaluation section
This is my biggest recommendation. The paper should avoid relying on pseudo-F1 as the main headline metric, or at least justify it much more carefully. Report standard metrics prominently and perhaps add a task-specific evaluation that better reflects practical utility.

2. Add annotation agreement and guideline detail
Especially for new type discovery, agreement on type induction/granularity is essential.

3. Strengthen controlled comparisons
Include more baselines with matched candidate generation and stronger generic embedding/clustering methods.

4. Expand analysis of the latent attribute module
Show sensitivity to K, examples of collapse, and perhaps quantitative coherence/diversity measures for latent attributes.

5. Clarify practical deployment story
Explain how discovered clusters would be surfaced to downstream systems, especially unnamed new clusters.

Recommendation

Weak Accept / Borderline

Rationale

I like the problem, the dataset contribution, and the practical orientation. The empirical results are encouraging, and the paper is generally well motivated. However, I have nontrivial reservations about the evaluation methodology and about how much of the gain is attributable to the core modeling ideas versus candidate generation and pipeline design. If accepted, I would encourage the authors to revise the evaluation framing and strengthen the analysis of annotation quality and latent-attribute behavior. Despite these concerns, I think the paper makes a useful contribution by pushing attribute mining toward a more realistic open-world weak-supervision setting.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting for e-commerce, where the goal is both to expand values for known seed attribute types and to discover entirely new attribute types without explicit type descriptions at inference time. The authors construct a new dataset, WoaM, spanning four Amazon product categories with a curated seed attribute set and human-annotated test data. They propose Amacer, a pipeline consisting of syntax-based candidate span generation, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for known attributes, DBSCAN-based clustering for remaining candidates, and two additional regularizers for unseen attributes: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive loss and an unsupervised latent-attribute topic-model-like objective. Experiments show substantial gains over closed-world tagging baselines and OA-Mine-style open-world baselines, with the best reported performance reaching 47.6 exact-match pseudo-F1 and 59.1 partial-match pseudo-F1, along with improved discovery of new attribute types.
strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored task setting: open-world attribute mining under limited supervision, beyond standard closed-world or zero-shot formulations.

The dataset contribution appears meaningful: WoaM includes titles and bullet points, multiple categories, curated seed attributes, and a substantial proportion of unseen attribute types and values, making the benchmark more realistic than prior title-only settings.
The proposed pipeline is well motivated and modular, with clear decomposition into candidate generation, representation learning, and grouping.
The syntax-based candidate generation is simple, scalable, and empirically stronger than segmentation-based alternatives in this setting.
The use of supervised contrastive learning for seed expansion is sensible and appears more effective than prior triplet/regression formulations.
The self-supervised and unsupervised regularization components are novel in this context and are supported by ablations showing gains, especially on new attribute discovery.
Experimental comparisons are fairly broad, including closed-world, segmentation-based open-world, and syntax-based variants, plus ablations isolating major components.
The paper includes useful quantitative breakdowns for seed vs. new attributes and title vs. bullet-point extraction, which help validate the claimed benefits on the intended hard cases.
The qualitative analysis is informative and candid, especially regarding failure modes on new attribute types and topic collapse in latent attributes.
weaknesses: The evaluation metric is somewhat unconventional: averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI into a pseudo-precision and then deriving a pseudo-F1 with recall is hard to interpret and may obscure practical extraction quality.
Span extraction quality remains fairly low, and much of the overall performance depends on candidate generation; this limits the practical readiness of the full system.
The dataset covers only four product categories, so it is unclear how well the approach generalizes to broader e-commerce domains or non-English settings.
The method relies on POS tagging quality and POS patterns derived from product profiles, which may be brittle under domain shift or noisy text.
The adaptive expansion thresholding heuristic is intuitive but somewhat ad hoc, and the paper does not deeply analyze its sensitivity or theoretical justification.

The latent attribute module is interesting but also complex relative to the gains; the paper acknowledges topic collapse and does not fully address whether the learned latent attributes are stable or necessary across settings.
Comparison to stronger modern alternatives, such as instruction-tuned LLM extraction or more recent span representation/clustering methods, is absent.
The seed set construction includes human curation and access to retailer-provided profiles; while lighter than full annotation, this may still be nontrivial in some deployment scenarios.
soundness_issues: The proposed task and method are generally coherent, and the empirical study supports the main claims, but some methodological choices weaken soundness.
The main evaluation metric is not standard and may not faithfully reflect end-task utility; conclusions based on pseudo-F1 should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

Because candidate generation and clustering are tightly coupled, improvements attributed to representation learning may partly reflect candidate quality differences; the gold-candidate analysis helps, but more controlled studies would strengthen the claim.

The self-supervised heuristic assumes spans in the same bullet point are semantically related and spans across bullet points within a product are less related; this is plausible but noisy, and the paper does not quantify when this assumption fails.

The latent attribute objective borrows from neural topic modeling, but the mapping from latent topics to attribute structure is only partially justified; repeated or collapsed latent attributes suggest the inductive bias is imperfect.
The paper reports statistical significance for the best scores, but details on variance, number of runs, and significance testing procedure are limited in the provided text.
Human annotation quality for the test set is not deeply discussed here (e.g., inter-annotator agreement), which matters because open-world span/type annotation is subjective.
